theme: Priest forever after the order of Melchizedek
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 110. It is only seven verses long, but it is the most quoted psalm in the New Testament. Read it slowly and mark the two oaths: God’s promise to make the king sit at his right hand, and his oath that the king is also a priest forever. Note how the Lord speaks to “my Lord.”
settingTheScene: David wrote this psalm, and Jesus himself used it to stump the religious leaders. In Mark 12:35-37, Jesus asked how David could call the Messiah “my Lord” if the Messiah was merely David’s son. The psalm contains a puzzle that is solved only in the person of Jesus. It pictures a king who is also a priest, which was forbidden in Israel, and who reigns at God’s right hand over his enemies. Hebrews returns to this psalm repeatedly. In the unit you are reading now, Psalm 110 is the foundation of the argument that Christ is a high priest after the order of Melchizedek.
observation: “The LORD says to my Lord” (v. 1). David, the king, speaks of another who is his Lord.
The Lord is told to sit at the right hand of God until his enemies are made his footstool (v. 1).
The scepter of the king will extend from Zion, and he will rule in the midst of his enemies (v. 2).
His people offer themselves freely on the day of his power, “in holy garments” (v. 3).
“The LORD has sworn and will not change his mind: You are a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek” (v. 4).
The Lord at God’s right hand will shatter kings on the day of his wrath and execute judgment among the nations (vv. 5-6).
The last verse is surprising: “He will drink from the brook by the way; therefore he will lift up his head” (v. 7).
The psalm combines two offices that never met in Israel, king and priest.
interpretation:
Psalm 110 is a royal psalm with an astonishing claim. The first verse is a conversation within God. “The LORD” (Yahweh) speaks to “my Lord” (Adonai), and invites him to sit at his right hand. David was the king of Israel, and no one was above him except God. So who is this Lord whom David calls his own? Jesus raised exactly this question, and the New Testament gives the answer: the Messiah is David’s son and David’s Lord. He is the descendant who is also the divine Son.

Verses 1-3 describe his reign. He sits at God’s right hand, the place of authority, until his enemies are subdued. The conquest does not depend on his strength alone, because the LORD himself puts the enemies under his feet. Yet verse 2 adds that he rules from Zion in the midst of his enemies. He is already reigning, even though his enemies are not yet fully defeated. This is the “already and not yet” of the kingdom. And verse 3 says his people will volunteer on the day of his power. They are not conscripted but willing, clothed in holiness.

Verse 4 is the center of the psalm. “The LORD has sworn and will not change his mind: You are a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek.” Two things stand out. First, God takes an oath. The Levitical priests were not appointed with an oath, but this priest is. Second, he is a priest forever, which means his priesthood has no end. The order of Melchizedek is not the Levitical order. It is the order of the priest-king who met Abraham in Genesis 14 and blessed him. This verse is the hinge of Hebrews 5-7. Hebrews argues that if there is a new priest of a different order, then the Levitical priesthood was never intended to be final.

The rest of the psalm describes judgment. The Lord at God’s right hand will shatter kings and fill the places with corpses. This language is graphic, and it is meant to be. The reign of Christ includes the defeat of every evil power. Yet the final image is not one of bloodshed but of weariness: he drinks from a brook along the way and lifts up his head. The conquering king pauses to drink. He is human, and his victory is won in a body that gets thirsty.

The psalm gathers the two great themes of the book of Hebrews: Christ is a king who reigns, and a priest who intercedes. He sits because his work is finished, and he reigns because his enemies will be subdued.
connection: Psalm 110:1 is quoted in Matthew 22:44, Acts 2:34-35, and Hebrews 1:13. Verse 4 is quoted in Hebrews 5:6, 7:17, and 7:21. The priest-king Melchizedek appears in Genesis 14:18-20, which you read in Unit 3. The Davidic promise of 2 Samuel 7 supports the royal side, and Zechariah 6:12-13 anticipates a priest who will sit and rule on his throne. The footstool imagery recalls Joshua 10:24 and 1 Corinthians 15:25.
application:
Pause to consider that the one who sits at God’s right hand is also the one who prays for you. The reigning king and the sympathetic priest are the same person. Whatever you are afraid of, he rules over it, and whatever you are ashamed of, he has covered it.

Think about being one of his willing people. Verse 3 says they offer themselves freely. What is one thing you could offer him freely this week, such as time, money, or an act of service?

And take courage in the final image. Your Lord is not a distant figure who never grew tired. He knows weariness, and he lifts his head in victory.
prayerPrompts: Bow to Jesus as your king and priest forever.
Thank him for the oath that cannot change.
Ask him to rule over what resists him in your life.
